The answer tells flu researchers whom to watch, random students or the friends they name. The natural guess is two and a half again. Every friend is one of these same eight girls. Check that on a rewired class where every girl has two friends. Send a token both ways along every friendship. Each token reads the friend count where it lands, always two. Both averages are two, the guess holds. Now restore the real friendships and send the tokens again. They read one, two, three, or four and averaged three. Every girl splits this way. Because the beam balances, the distances add to zero, and the cross terms cancel. So the average of k squared is mu squared plus sigma squared. And friends average mu plus sigma squared over mu. Here that's two and a half, plus a half, exactly the extra half friend we measured. With no spread, the ring had no gap. In 2011, Facebook users averaged about 190 friends, and a few had thousands. If every friendship sent tokens, what would the tokens average? About 635. The spread term is more than twice the mean. The friends curve rose first. Fitted curves put them 13.9 days ahead. With self-reported symptoms, the lead shrank to about three. Betty looks at her one friend. Sue and sees four.
